title: Initializers and properties (lazy, computed, observers, wrappers)
summary: Every stored property must have a value before an object is used. Swift gives several kinds of properties: stored, computed, lazy, with observers, or wrapped by a property wrapper.
body: **In simple words:** An initializer (`init`) prepares a new value so that every property has a value. Swift refuses to compile code that could read an uninitialized property.

**Structs:** get a free memberwise init (`User(name:age:)`). **Classes:** have **designated** inits (fully set up this class and call `super.init`) and **convenience** inits (shortcuts that must call another init of the same class). A `required` init must be implemented by every subclass. A **failable** init (`init?`) returns `nil` when input is invalid.

**Two-phase init for classes:** phase 1 - every class in the chain sets its own stored properties (subclass first, then `super.init`). Phase 2 - now `self` is fully ready and methods can be called. This is why you cannot call `self.method()` before `super.init`.

**Kinds of properties:** stored (`var name`), computed (`var fullName: String { first + " " + last }` - calculated on every read, no storage), `lazy var` (calculated on first use, good for expensive setup; not thread-safe), observers (`willSet`/`didSet` run when the value changes), and `static` (one per type, lazily created and thread-safe).
**Property wrappers** move repeated get/set logic into a reusable type: `@Published`, `@AppStorage`, `@State` are all property wrappers. You can write your own, e.g. `@Clamped(0...100) var volume`.
keyPoints: All stored properties must be set before use; Swift enforces it at compile time.
Designated inits call `super.init`; convenience inits call `self.init`.
Two-phase init: set own properties, call super, then use `self`.
`lazy` = computed once on first access; computed = every access; `static let` = lazily created once and thread-safe (good for singletons).
Property wrappers package reusable property behavior (`wrappedValue`, `projectedValue` accessed with `$`).

code.caption: Failable init, lazy, observers and a property wrapper

mistakes: Expecting `didSet` to run during `init` - it does not for the class's own properties.
Using `lazy var` from several threads at once - it can initialize twice.
Doing heavy work in a computed property that is read many times (e.g. inside SwiftUI `body`).
followups: **Why must a subclass call `super.init`?** So the parent's stored properties get set up (phase 1).
**Can a struct have a convenience init?** No keyword needed; add extra inits in an extension to keep the free memberwise init.
**What is `$` on a property wrapper?** The `projectedValue`, e.g. `$text` is a `Binding` for `@State`.
